subject: woodcutRaven
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: raven on a skull.
Style: woodcut print.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a woodcut-style raven perched on a skull, using a limited black-ink-on-cream palette with hatching lines for texture, feather strokes on the raven, and shadow hatching on the skull.

I'm roughing out proportions: a slightly stylized skull around 0.24m high with a raven perched on top totaling roughly 0.75m, with the skull resting stably on the ground via its jaw.

For rigging, I'm deciding on the raven's rest pose — rather than fully folded wings, I'll go with a half-open, mantling-style spread for more dramatic woodcut readability, building out a shoulder-elbow-wrist joint chain with fanning primary feathers at the wingtip.

Writing wing feather geometry...

For the woodcut raven look, I'm thinking through how to paint carved white lines over black ink based on lighting — stripe phase determined by position along a direction vector, with line width scaled by how directly lit the surface is, so lit areas show denser carved lines while shadowed areas stay solid black.

Working through texel resolution for the paint atlas — settling on 2048 for finer detail with the body's hatch lines following the feather flow direction (head to tail along the tube), using the angle-based sweep coordinate to drive the stripe phase.

For feathers, I'm planning the extruded geometry so lines run along the shaft axis while barbs sit diagonally, with the rachis rendered as a narrow centered highlight band.

For the skull, I'm shading with cream-colored paper as the base and layering ink hatching and cross-hatching where the light contribution drops, plus cracks and noise stippling for texture. The eye sockets become dark hollow ellipsoids with a decal ring, the nasal cavity is an inverted heart-shaped cutout, and teeth are small boxes placed along the jaw and mandible.

Now I'm planning the joint hierarchy: a single root joint called "skull" positioned at the skull's center, with a "jaw" joint as its child hinged at the rear, and the raven's joints (hips, etc.) also attached as children of the skull root since it's perched there.

Then I'm assigning roles to each joint — spine, neck, head, and jaw — and making sure names stay unique between the skull's jaw and the raven's lower beak jaw. Next I'm thinking through the overall geometry orientation, with the model and skull facing +Z while the raven may be turned slightly.

Working out skull dimensions now: placing the cranium sphere center and radii to set the top of the skull, with the mandible resting at y=0.

Then I'm mapping the face region, positioning eye sockets, nasal bridge, and upper teeth coordinates, and sketching the mandible as a U-shaped sweep path from hinge to chin with mirrored symmetry.

Tuning the sweep's circular cross-section radius so the bottom sits flush at y=0, and planning to share the skull's paint shading across the sweep. For teeth, I'm thinking of placing small boxes along the maxilla and mandible paths with a loop.

Positioning upper and lower tooth rows as arcs along a curve, with the upper teeth hanging from the skull around y=0.073-0.09 and lower teeth sitting on the mandible around y=0.026-0.04, using the same paint style as the skull for cohesion.

Still shaping the skull geometry...

Checking the cranium front surface position against the eye socket placement, I realize the socket as a plain sphere would poke out through the face surface since its radius extends further than the cranium curvature allows. I need a different approach — making the sockets read as indentations rather than protrusions, perhaps by sinking a dark sphere mostly inside the cranium surface instead of centering it right at the surface.

I'm working out the eye socket geometry, balancing a cream-colored rim torus against a dark recessed disc so the depth reads correctly against the angled skull surface — settling on a simple dark sphere scaled into an ellipsoid that protrudes slightly to suggest the socket's shadow.

Now I'm figuring out how to position these sockets accurately using surface hit-testing against the cranium mesh, computing the azimuth and elevation angles from a given center point so each socket seats naturally on the curved surface rather than floating above it.

For the nasal cavity, I'm placing a small inverted-heart-shaped dark extrusion near the front of the maxilla, built from a simple outline with a thin extrude depth so it sits slightly proud of the front face.

Next I'm thinking through surface details like crack lines and suture patterns on the cranium -- draping zigzag or catmull curves onto the skull surface and sweeping thin ink strokes along them to add texture, like a coronal suture line across the top.

I need to set up the jaw joint hinge position and aim direction for the mandible, plus teeth placement on the jaw bone. I'm deciding to skip extra flourishes like an engraved inscription or forehead marking, keeping the skull detail focused, and now moving on to the raven.

The raven perches atop the skull's crown, so I'm working out its foot placement, body proportions (length, stand height, leg length), and overall posture angle for a natural perched stance, then sketching the spine path from tail to body center in side view.

Now I'm plotting out the skeleton points along the spine from hips to chest with a forward tilt, then continuing up through the neck to the head, defining the head's position, size, and the thick forward-pointing beak typical of a stylized raven.

For the tail, I'm working out points trailing back and down from the rump, checking that it clears the skull's back edge so it hangs freely behind without overlapping, matching the wedge-shaped tail characteristic of ravens with roughly 7 feather blades.

Now I'm figuring out the geometry for fanning those feathers horizontally from the rump, with central feathers longest to create the wedge shape, computing the width direction for each feather as perpendicular to its extrusion direction within the tail's plane.

Now I'm designing the feather outline shape as a function taking length and half-width, plotting curve points along the quill with a tapered, slightly squared tip to mimic raven primary feathers.

To avoid z-fighting where overlapping feathers share a plane, I'm offsetting each feather layer slightly along its normal based on stacking order.

Now I'm working out the wing geometry for the left side, positioning shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints to create a half-open, mantled pose like a raven about to take flight, with wings extended outward and drooping slightly.

Still computing wing geometry...

Computing the backward chord vector confirms the orthogonal basis works out correctly. Now I'm working out the fan angle for the primary feathers, spacing them from a sharply forward leading angle back to around 55°, with lengths tapering along that spread.

I'm now plotting root positions for the primaries along the hand/wrist and then placing the secondary feathers along the forearm trailing edge, angling them close to perpendicular to the wing's spine.

I'm layering coverts above the flight feathers: greater and medium covert rows along the arm, plus denser primary coverts at the wrist, offset slightly above the secondaries and primaries for depth. Then I'm structuring the wing skeleton itself, defining a joint chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist to hand tip to anchor each feather group.

Still writing joint logic...

Working out the frame orientation for the arm's radius function... I need to figure out which local axis corresponds to fore-aft width versus vertical thickness, reasoning through the tangent/normal/binormal setup for a sideways-pointing bone with world-up as the normal reference.

For wing coverage, I'm deciding to skip a membrane layer and instead rely on dense overlapping feather rows (secondaries plus coverts) to avoid gaps — checking that feather spacing along the arm and angular spacing for primaries both keep adjacent feathers overlapping so no see-through holes appear.

Working out the primaries fanning from the wrist outward with coverts covering their base, adjusting the angle range so the gap between secondaries and primaries closes smoothly near the wrist joint.

Now I'm shaping the raven's head and beak - a thick, slightly curved beak with a bezier-curved upper mandible tapering from a wider base to a sharp tip, plus a slimmer lower beak hinged at the jaw.

For the eyes, I'm designing a woodcut-style decal with a dark pupil and a cream highlight ring, placed onto the head surface using surface coordinates around the head's center.

For the brow ridge I'm sticking a small flattened sphere above the eye socket for a subtle wedge shape, and for the throat I'm planning shaggy raven hackle feathers using scattered feather-tuft card textures across the throat, neck ruff, and breast regions, drawn as pointed black tufts with engraved cream woodcut lines.

Now I'm designing the body structure as a spine chain running from hips through the ribcage toward the neck and head, setting up the hips as the root joint positioned below the skull with a forward-upward orientation, then building out the spine chain joints from rump to chest.

Still defining joint chains...

I'm shaping the body with a pear-like radius profile (narrow rump, wider chest), then connecting a tapered neck sweep bound to the spine/neck bones, and placing the head sphere near the top of the neck.

Now I'm working out the beak geometry: positioning its base and tip coordinates, then curving the upper beak with a quadratic bezier to get that heavy, downward-swooping raven profile with tapering radii along its length.

Still defining bone joints...

Checking the tail clears the skull geometry at that height and depth—looks fine. I'll attach each feather to the tail chain based on its position, mostly rigging to the second tail bone, and taper the tail base thickness for the undertail coverts using a flattened radius profile along the chain.

Now I'm working out the legs: hidden thighs inside the body, visible tarsus segments about 0.07 long and thick, with three forward toes and one back toe gripping the top of the skull. I'm computing where the feet should sit on the cranium surface by solving the ellipsoid equation for y at the foot's x,z position.

I'm working out the leg geometry with hip and ankle positions roughly 0.123 apart, using two segments of about 0.075 and 0.07 to span that distance with a forward knee bend, since birds' knees fold forward and stay hidden while the visible hock joint projects backward.

I'm naming the leg joints (hip, knee, hock, foot) and mirroring them with L/R suffixes based on X position, parented under hips. Now I'm thinking through how to rig the toes—three front digits plus a hind hallux—likely as small sprout chains off the foot joint.

For the toes, I'm planning eight small chains (four per foot, two joints each) sweeping forward and slightly down from the ankle, making sure the tips curve to drape naturally over the cranium's surface without clipping into it.

I should add a fallback for when the ray misses so the point still resolves. For the toe chain itself, I'll build it with a catmull spline through the sample points, sweeping a tapering radius with round caps, then cap each toe with a small dark cone as a claw oriented along the end tangent. I'll keep the foot mostly ink-black but add thin white contour lines so it reads against the cranium in the woodcut style, and leave the ground background empty.

I'm settling on the print's palette: deep ink black and warm cream paper, with a muted mid-tone for shading and a small rust-red accent reserved for the raven's eye ring and nasal area to give it that hand-tinted antique look. Now I'm defining the lighting direction vector for the paint/shading functions.

Writing the hatching shader...

I'm adding a crosshatch pattern for strong shadows using a second diagonal direction, plus fine stipple noise to simulate ink speckles for pits. I'm also working out the texel density needed based on the painted surface area of the raven's body and feathers.

Now I'm starting the paint function for the raven itself, which will combine black base coloring with white cut lines following the feather rows, driven by the light dot product.

Still writing feather scale logic...

Working out barb line widths and spacing, with top faces lit and underside faces falling into shadow so the form reads in black and cream. I'm splitting the painting logic into two separate functions—one for body sweeps, one for feather extrudes—since each needs a different surface parameterization.

For the head's sphere geometry, uv-based coordinates don't map cleanly to the feather line logic, so I want a position-based paint function driven by world position and normal instead, usable consistently across body and non-tube parts. Rather than cell-based blotches, I'm leaning toward contour hatching: lines following a family of planes cut perpendicular to the body's direction of travel.

For the raven specifically, I'm designing white gouge-style hatch lines against black, oriented along the body's head-to-tail axis so they follow the feather flow and curve naturally around the form, brightening where lit.

I'm also planning the beak color as a slightly lighter ink tone, scaly ring-based textures for the legs, and separate paint definitions for feathers and skull shading. Now I'm starting an SVG for throat hackle feathers—a pointed black feather shape with cream line details.

Working out stroke widths and viewBox scale...

Now I'm figuring out card placement across the bird: throat cards filtered to the underside front of the head sphere, neck hackle cards scattered along the neck sweep, and larger breast feather cards on the body, each set with its own size range, lean angle, and flow direction leaning backward and down.

I'll keep the texture count reasonable, mixing pointed and round feather tufts for variety alongside the raven eye decal, and considering whether to add a small carved sigil detail on the skull's forehead for extra character.

Starting the TypeScript builder code...

Setting up the color palette with rust tones, then building a helper for vectors and initializing the builder for the raven-on-skull rig, starting with the skull joint and thinking through role naming for head joints.

Now I'm defining the jaw joint hierarchy, deciding to name the skull's jaw "jaw" and the raven's lower beak "beakLower" with a jaw role to keep naming consistent across the rig. I need a surface query helper to find outer-shell hit points for placing orbit sockets and face pieces, computing directions from the cranium center so I can position the eye sockets and frustum-shaped face box relative to the skull's actual geometry rather than guessing coordinates.

Checking whether the orbit socket's ellipsoid actually overlaps the maxilla box geometrically — the socket radius and position seem to put it right at the boundary where the maxilla's front face could partially occlude it, depending on exact half-widths at that z-depth.

It extends slightly beyond the box, which is fine visually. I'll adjust socket angle and narrow the maxilla width slightly, then add cheek arch rods as capsule shapes connecting near the jaw joint hinge. Now I'm starting the mandible sweep path using a Catmull curve through several points.

Simplifying to a constant radius for the jaw cross-section, then working out tooth placement along the chin's curved arc, positioning upper and lower rows with their vertical centers and spacing based on that curve.

Checking the box widths line up against the arc curve at each tooth position, confirming they stay roughly within bounds. I'm deciding whether to keep teeth as separate parts (18 total) or merge geometries for simplicity.

For the sutures, I'm settling on a coronal suture at z=0 and a sagittal suture along the x=0 plane, each generated as a slice of the full ring.

Adding zigzag crack logic...

I'm working out the rotation math to confirm the torus axis aligns with the normal direction, then adding a helper function that retrieves a hit point from a socket at given azimuth/elevation and throws if none found, plus planning the nasal cavity extrusion and forehead sigil decal.

Now I'm sketching out a raven eye SVG texture, using concentric circles for the dark outer rim, light ring, and pupil to mimic a woodcut-style eye.

For the head, I'm building the sphere geometry with scaled proportions for the skull shape, then planning brow ridges and a beak-base bump with small spike-like nasal bristle tufts.

I'm skipping the nostril groove detail since the bristle covers it. For the lower beak, I'm defining a joint between two points and giving it a slight rotation so the mouth sits in a subtle open pose, pairing it with a small jaw-open rotation on the skull so the creature looks like it's mid-croak — applying both poses after all parts are built so the deformation holds correctly, and double-checking the rotation doesn't push the mandible below the ground plane.

I need to verify the hinge rotation angle carefully: checking how far the chin drops when rotating around the jaw hinge at various degrees, since too much rotation pushes the lowest point below the 2% tolerance threshold for the model's height. After running the math, 6° drops too close to the limit, so I'm settling on a smaller 5° rotation to keep the chin comfortably within bounds while still giving a slightly open mouth look.

Now I'm shifting to designing a generic feather-placement function for the wings, where each feather gets oriented using its root position, direction vector, and surface normal, computing a perpendicular width axis via cross product so the feather's thickness properly aligns with the wing surface normal.

I'm defining the Joint type and closing all helper functions over the builder instance inside the main build function, keeping everything scoped together even though the function grows long.

Writing extrude parameters...

I'm estimating triangle counts and feather totals: roughly 45 feathers per wing across primaries, secondaries, and coverts, plus tail feathers, bringing the total part count to around 250, with triangle counts staying manageable at scale.

Writing feather paint function...

Checking the barb line direction against the constant formula to confirm they sweep outward and toward the tip as intended.

Now I'm computing the cut width based on lighting direction—wider fractions for lit top faces, narrower for underside shading—then using a fractional distance function to define the stripe pattern along each barb.

I'm checking that the hatch spacing (~0.007) still resolves at texel resolution, needing roughly six texels per period so the cut width stays above ~0.17, and sizing feather lengths accordingly.

I'm considering restricting the scale arcs to only the brighter regions to cut the cost, but then I notice a flaw: since the cut lines are built from a coordinate based on world x, on the sides of the body where the surface normal is roughly aligned with x, those planes run parallel to the surface and the lines degenerate into oversized patches instead of proper contours.

To fix this I'm picking a hatching direction that depends on which axis of the normal dominates, so the line family only degenerates near a single singular point rather than across whole surface regions — similar to how real woodcut hatching avoids running parallel to broad flat faces. I'm working out the exact blend of x, y, z coordinates to use for each dominant-normal case so the stripes stay visually consistent across different surface orientations.
